title: جَمْع الْمُذَكَّر السَّالِم Across the Cases: Why مُسْلِمُونَ Becomes مُسْلِمِينَ
summary: After a long break the class returns to one point the teacher felt had been rushed: the sound masculine plural shows its case by a letter rather than a vowel. مُسْلِمُونَ stands where a ḍamma would go and مُسْلِمِينَ where a fatḥa or kasra would — exactly the logic of طَالِبَانِ and طَالِبَيْنِ from the dual. The lesson is then reread with that in mind, and every مُدَرِّسُون and مُدَرِّسِين in the dialogue is justified out loud: مُضَاف إِلَيْه, مَفْعُول بِه, counted noun, خَبَر, فَاعِل. Along the way the class separates sound plurals from broken ones, learns that this plural belongs only to rational beings, and finds out why so many of these words begin with a مِيم.
key_points: The lesson's one real point: جَمْع الْمُذَكَّر السَّالِم marks its case with a letter, not a ḥarakah — وْن where the word would take a ḍamma, يْن where it would take a fatḥa or a kasra. So مُسْلِمُونَ، مُؤْمِنُونَ، مُتَّقُونَ beside مُسْلِمِينَ، مُؤْمِنِينَ، مُتَّقِينَ.
It is the same mechanism as the dual learned in the previous lesson: طَالِبَانِ in the ḍamma position, طَالِبَيْنِ in the fatḥa or kasra position. Both still mean two students.

Never read the case off the last letter — the نُون carries a fatḥa either way. Look at the letter before it: a وَاو means the ḍamma position, a يَاء means either fatḥa or kasra, and the context decides which.
The feminine counterpart, جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم, simply adds ات: مُسْلِمَات، مُؤْمِنَات، قَانِتَات، مُدَرِّسَات.

سَالِم means sound, or unbroken: the plural only adds to the word and leaves it intact. A جَمْع تَكْسِير rearranges it — رَجُل becomes رِجَال, قَلَم becomes أَقْلَام, طَالِب becomes طُلَّاب, هِنْدِيّ becomes هُنُود, كَافِر becomes كُفَّار.
Some words carry both plurals, and both occur in the Qur'an: طَالِبُون beside طُلَّاب, كَافِرُون beside كُفَّار, صَالِحُون beside صُلَحَاء.
This plural belongs only to the عَاقِل, to rational beings. أُسْبُوع has no sound plural — its plural is أَسَابِيع — so أُسْبُوعَيْنِ in the exercise is the dual, two weeks, not a plural.
The tens behave the same way: عِشْرُون and عِشْرِين، ثَلَاثُون، أَرْبَعُون، خَمْسُون، سِتُّون، سَبْعُون، ثَمَانُون، تِسْعُون, each switching to the يَاء form in a fatḥa or kasra position.

Every instance in the dialogue is reasoned from its grammar rather than memorised: غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ (مُضَاف إِلَيْه, so a kasra position), أَرَأَيْتَ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ الْجُدُدَ (مَفْعُول بِه, with الْجُدُد as its صِفَة following it), خَمْسَةُ مُدَرِّسِينَ (the counted noun as مُضَاف إِلَيْه), هُمْ غَائِبُونَ (خَبَر, so the وَاو), and سَبْعٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ صَفْحَةً for the pages remaining, where the tens word is the فَاعِل of بَقِيَ and so keeps the وَاو.

لَا can replace مَا for negating a past verb when two things are negated together — the teacher's evidence being فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى, so the dialogue's neither-entered-nor-are-they-present takes لَا.

أل only makes a word definite; it never changes the ḥarakah. Leaving it off changes the meaning instead: asking whether مُدَرِّسُونَ جُدُدٌ have come expresses surprise that new teachers exist at all, where الْمُدَرِّسُونَ الْجُدُد would take their existence for granted and ask only about their arrival.

Why so many of these plurals begin with مِيم: they are أَسْمَاء الْفَاعِل. A three-letter verb gives the فَاعِل pattern — صَائِم، ضَارِب، قَاتِل، غَائِب — while a verb of more than three letters replaces the يُـ of its مُضَارِع with مُـ: يُجْتَهِدُ gives مُجْتَهِد, يُجَاهِدُ gives مُجَاهِد, يُصَلِّي gives مُصَلِّي, يُدَرِّسُ gives مُدَرِّس, يُعَلِّمُ gives مُعَلِّم, يُؤْمِنُ gives مُؤْمِن, and يُسْلِمُ gives مُسْلِم.

A نَصْب that does not show a fatḥa: الْمُسْلِمَاتِ as an object is مَنْصُوب yet not مَفْتُوح, because here the نَصْب appears as a kasra. The teacher named the distinction and then set it aside, keeping the class at the level it needs to read the Qur'an rather than full grammatical terminology.

Vocabulary and dialogue: غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِين (the teachers' room, a staff lounge), اجْتِمَاع (a gathering, here a meeting), جُدُد (new, plural), حَقِيبَة (a bag), أَصْغَر مِنْهَا (smaller than it), رِيَال, and the reader قِصَصُ النَّبِيِّين by Fadīlat al-Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī al-Nadwī — قِصَص being the plural of قِصَّة.
Homework: tamrīn nine and eleven, both asking for the numbers to be written out in letters so the ون and ين forms have to be chosen correctly. The class resumes Monday.
questions: [00:00:55] Q: What is this type of plural called? — A: جَمْع الْمُذَكَّر السَّالِم; its feminine counterpart is جَمْع الْمُؤَنَّث السَّالِم, which adds ات to give مُسْلِمَات، مُؤْمِنَات، قَانِتَات.

[00:02:03] Q: Why do we sometimes see مُسْلِمُون and sometimes مُسْلِمِين، مُؤْمِنِين، مُتَّقِين? — A: For the same reason طَالِبَانِ becomes طَالِبَيْنِ — the وَاو form stands in the ḍamma position and the يَاء form in a fatḥa or kasra position.
[00:05:20] Q: Why is it مُدَرِّسِين in غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ but مُدَرِّسُون earlier in the passage? — A: Here it is the مُضَاف إِلَيْه, which takes a kasra, so the plural shows its يَاء form.

[00:05:55] Q: Why is لَا used here, when a past-tense verb is normally negated with مَا? — A: Because two things are being negated together, which Arabic does with لَا, as in فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى — neither did they enter the classroom nor are they in the teachers' room.
[00:06:50] Q: What does اجْتِمَاع mean? — A: A gathering of people; in this context, a meeting.

[00:07:40] Q: Is الْمُدَرِّسِينَ in أَرَأَيْتَ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ الْجُدُدَ in that form because of the أل? — A: No. أل only makes a word definite and never changes the ḥarakah. It is the مَفْعُول بِه of أَرَأَيْتَ, and the object takes a fatḥa.
[00:08:15] Q: And why does الْجُدُدَ carry a fatḥa? — A: It is the صِفَة of الْمُدَرِّسِين, so it follows the word it describes.
[00:09:50] Q: Why خَمْسَةُ مُدَرِّسِينَ rather than مُدَرِّسُون? — A: By the rules of number: the counted noun becomes the مُضَاف إِلَيْه and takes a kasra, which gives the يَاء form.
[00:25:15] Q: Can one word have both a sound and a broken plural? — A: Yes. طَالِبُون and طُلَّاب are both used, as are كَافِرُون and كُفَّار; either is acceptable.

[00:28:00] Q: How do we know أُسْبُوعَيْنِ is not a جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم? — A: Because that plural is used only for the عَاقِل, and أُسْبُوع is not; its plural is أَسَابِيع. So this is the dual — two weeks.

[00:32:20] Q: What is the reason for the مِيم at the front of so many of these words? — A: They are أَسْمَاء الْفَاعِل of verbs longer than three letters, formed by replacing the يُـ of the مُضَارِع with مُـ, as يُدَرِّسُ gives مُدَرِّس and يُؤْمِنُ gives مُؤْمِن.

[00:38:10] Q: Are عِشْرُون and عِشْرِين interchangeable, or is one more correct? — A: Generally they are the same word in two states, and are often used interchangeably, though grammatically they are not identical — a distinction the teacher deliberately leaves aside.

[00:38:50] Q: Is الْمُسْلِمَاتِ مَفْتُوح when it is the object? — A: It is مَنْصُوب but not مَفْتُوح. In this case the نَصْب shows as a kasra rather than a fatḥa, which is why the two terms are not the same thing.

quiz.q: When does مُسْلِم take the form مُسْلِمُونَ rather than مُسْلِمِينَ?
options: Where the word would otherwise take a ḍamma
Where the word would otherwise take a fatḥa or kasra
Only at the beginning of a sentence
They are freely interchangeable
quiz.a: The وَاو form stands in for the ḍamma; the يَاء form covers both the fatḥa and the kasra positions.

quiz.q: In a جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم, which letter tells you the case?
options: The final نُون
The ḥarakah on the final نُون
The letter before the نُون — a وَاو or a يَاء
The first letter of the word
quiz.a: The نُون carries a fatḥa either way, so it tells you nothing. The وَاو means the ḍamma position and the يَاء means a fatḥa or kasra position.

quiz.q: Why is it غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ and not غُرْفَةُ الْمُدَرِّسُونَ?
options: Because of the أل
Because it is the مُضَاف إِلَيْه, a kasra position
Because غُرْفَة is feminine
Because it is the فَاعِل
quiz.a: The second term of an إِضَافَة takes a kasra, and for this plural a kasra position shows as the يَاء form.

quiz.q: Which of these is a جَمْع تَكْسِير, a broken plural?
options: مُدَرِّسُون
طُلَّاب
مُسْلِمَات
مُهَنْدِسُون
quiz.a: طَالِب is rearranged to give طُلَّاب, so the word itself is broken. A sound plural only adds to the word and leaves it intact.

quiz.q: Why is أُسْبُوعَيْنِ not a جَمْع مُذَكَّر سَالِم?
options: Because its plural is أَسَابِيع and this plural is only for rational beings — so this is the dual
Because it begins with a hamza
Because it is feminine
Because it has no plural at all
quiz.a: جَمْع الْمُذَكَّر السَّالِم belongs to the عَاقِل. أُسْبُوع takes the broken plural أَسَابِيع, so أُسْبُوعَيْنِ here means two weeks.

quiz.q: In هُمْ غَائِبُونَ, why غَائِبُونَ rather than غَائِبِينَ?
options: Because it is the مَفْعُول بِه
Because it follows هُمْ
Because it is the خَبَر, which takes a ḍamma
Because غَائِب has no يَاء form
quiz.a: The خَبَر is a ḍamma position, and for this plural that shows as the وَاو.

quiz.q: Why does the dialogue negate the past verbs with لَا instead of مَا?
options: Because مَا is only for the present
Because two things are being negated together
Because the subject is plural
Because لَا is more emphatic
quiz.a: The teacher's evidence is فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى — when a pair of things is negated, Arabic uses لَا even in the past.

quiz.q: What effect does أل have on a word's ḥarakah?
options: It makes the word take a ḍamma
It makes the word take a fatḥa
None — it only makes the word definite
It removes the ḥarakah entirely
quiz.a: A student assumed أل was behind the fatḥa in أَرَأَيْتَ الْمُدَرِّسِينَ الْجُدُدَ; in fact the case comes from being the object of أَرَأَيْتَ.

quiz.q: How is the اسْم الْفَاعِل formed from a verb of more than three letters?
options: On the pattern of فَاعِل
By replacing the يُـ of the مُضَارِع with مُـ
By adding ون to the end
By breaking the word
quiz.a: يُدَرِّسُ gives مُدَرِّس, يُجَاهِدُ gives مُجَاهِد, يُسْلِمُ gives مُسْلِم — which is why so many of these plurals open with a مِيم. Three-letter verbs instead give صَائِم، ضَارِب، غَائِب.

quiz.q: The remaining pages are سَبْعٌ وَثَلَاثُونَ صَفْحَةً. Why ثَلَاثُونَ and not ثَلَاثِينَ?
options: Because it is the فَاعِل of بَقِيَ, a ḍamma position
Because it is the مَفْعُول بِه
Because numbers are always in the وَاو form
Because صَفْحَة is feminine
quiz.a: What remains is the pages, so the number is the doer of بَقِيَ and sits in a ḍamma position, giving the وَاو form. Of the ninety pages, fifty-three were read — ثَلَاثٌ وَخَمْسُونَ — leaving thirty-seven.

quran_examples.arabic: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْمُسْلِمَاتِ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ وَالْقَانِتِينَ وَالْقَانِتَاتِ
quran_examples.transliteration: inna l-muslimīna wa-l-muslimāti wa-l-muʾminīna wa-l-muʾmināti wa-l-qānitīna wa-l-qānitāti
quran_examples.translation: Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the obedient men and obedient women…
quran_examples.note: Both sound plurals in one verse, paired again and again. The masculine forms take the يَاء because إِنَّ puts them in the نَصْب position, and the feminine forms are exactly the مُسْلِمَات and قَانِتَات the teacher gave as examples.

quran_examples.translation: Certainly will the believers have succeeded.
quran_examples.note: The same word in the other state: as the فَاعِل of أَفْلَحَ it sits in a ḍamma position, so it appears with the وَاو as الْمُؤْمِنُونَ.

quran_examples.translation: Indeed, the righteous will be within gardens and springs.
quran_examples.note: The مُتَّقُون / مُتَّقِين pair the teacher raised at the start. After إِنَّ the word is مَنْصُوب, which this plural shows by the يَاء rather than by a fatḥa.

quran_examples.translation: …and they killed the prophets without right.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's own citation for النَّبِيِّين while reading قِصَصُ النَّبِيِّين: as the object of يَقْتُلُونَ it takes the يَاء form, against النَّبِيُّون in a ḍamma position.
The evidence for negating a past verb with لَا instead of مَا: two things are denied together, which is the construction the lesson's dialogue uses.
